sections.heading: Earth in the solar system & motions of the Earth

blocks.text: The **Earth** is the **third planet** from the Sun and the only known abode of life. Its two motions — **rotation (on its axis)** and **revolution (around the Sun)** — produce **day-night and the seasons**, and its **tilt (23.5°)** governs the pattern of insolation.

rows: Earth spins **west→east** in ~**23 hrs 56 min**; causes **day & night**, the **Coriolis force**, and tides timing.
Earth orbits the Sun in **365¼ days**; with the axial tilt causes **seasons**; leap year adjusts the ¼ day.
**23.5°** to the orbital plane — the cause of seasons & varying day length.

sections.heading: 🔎 Exam-ready deep coverage: solar system & Earth's motions

items: **Solar system**: **8 planets** (Mercury→Neptune); inner **terrestrial/rocky** (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars) vs outer **Jovian/gas giants** (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune); **asteroid belt** between Mars & Jupiter; **Pluto = dwarf planet (2006, IAU)**; **Sun = 99.8% of system mass**, plasma of H+He.

**Earth ('Blue/Goldilocks planet')**: densest planet; only one with life/liquid water; **Venus** = hottest (runaway greenhouse) & Earth's 'twin'; **Jupiter** = largest; **Saturn** = rings/lowest density (floats on water).
**Rotation (24 hrs, W→E)** → day & night, ~15°/hour, deflection of winds/currents (**Coriolis force**), difference in local time (**1° = 4 minutes**).
**Revolution (365¼ days)** + **axial tilt of 23.5°** → **seasons**; the extra ¼ day → **leap year**.

**Key positions**: **Summer solstice (21 June — Sun over Tropic of Cancer)**, **Winter solstice (22 Dec — Tropic of Capricorn)**, **Equinoxes (21 Mar & 23 Sep — Sun over Equator, equal day-night)**; **perihelion (~3 Jan, nearest)**, **aphelion (~4 July, farthest)**.

blocks.text: Prelims trap: it is the **axial tilt (23.5°) + revolution**, not the Earth-Sun distance, that causes seasons (Earth is actually nearest the Sun in January).

items: Rotation → day/night & Coriolis; revolution + 23.5° tilt → seasons.
Perihelion (~3 Jan) vs Aphelion (~4 July); terrestrial vs Jovian planets.

prelimsPointers: Earth — **3rd planet**; rotation **west→east**, ~**23 hr 56 min** (sidereal day).
**Axial tilt = 23.5°** — the cause of seasons.
**Revolution** ~**365¼ days**; the extra ¼ day gives a **leap year**.
**Perihelion ~3 January**, **Aphelion ~4 July**.
Terrestrial (inner, rocky) vs **Jovian (outer, gaseous)** planets.
Rotation causes the **Coriolis force** (deflection — right in N hemisphere, left in S).
**Equinoxes** (21 Mar, 23 Sep) — equal day & night; **Solstices** (21 Jun, 22 Dec).
**Terrestrial** planets (Mercury-Venus-Earth-Mars) vs **Jovian** gas giants; **Pluto = dwarf planet (2006)**.
**Venus** = hottest & Earth's twin; **Jupiter** = largest; **Saturn** = least dense.
Rotation → day/night & **Coriolis**; **1° longitude = 4 min** of time.
**Solstices**: 21 June (Cancer), 22 Dec (Capricorn); **equinoxes** 21 Mar & 23 Sep.
**Perihelion ~3 Jan; Aphelion ~4 July**; axial tilt **23.5°** causes seasons.

glossary.definition: The Earth's spin on its own axis (west to east), causing day and night.
The Earth's orbit around the Sun, which with the axial tilt causes the seasons.
The apparent deflection of moving objects/winds due to the Earth's rotation.

blocks.text: **Time** is measured by the Earth's rotation via **longitudes**, giving **local and standard time and time zones**, while the **seasons** result from the Earth's revolution and axial tilt shifting the Sun's vertical rays between the tropics.

rows: **360° / 24 hrs → 15°/hour; 1° = 4 minutes**; places east are ahead.
**~180° International Date Line** — date changes; zig-zags to avoid landmasses.
Sun overhead at **Tropic of Cancer (~21 Jun, N summer)**, **Equator (equinoxes)**, **Tropic of Capricorn (~22 Dec)**.

sections.heading: 🔎 Exam-ready deep coverage: time zones & seasons

items: **Longitude & time**: Earth rotates **360° in 24 hrs → 15°/hour → 1° = 4 minutes**; places **east are ahead** in time. The **Prime Meridian (0°, Greenwich)** = **GMT/UTC** reference.
**International Date Line (~180°)**: crossing **W→E → subtract a day**; **E→W → add a day**; it zig-zags to avoid landmasses (Aleutians, Fiji, etc.).
**Indian Standard Time (IST)** = **82°30'E** (Mirzapur, near Allahabad) = **GMT +5:30**; India spans ~29° longitude but keeps a single time zone.

**Seasons cause (Northern Hemisphere)**: tilt makes the N-pole lean toward the Sun in June (summer) & away in December (winter); the tropics get vertical sun twice a year, the poles have **6-month day/night**; **midnight sun** & polar night.
**Twilight** longer at the poles; the **circle of illumination** divides day & night.
1° longitude = 4 minutes; IST = 82.5°E = GMT +5:30.
IDL ≈ 180°; solstices/equinoxes drive the seasons.

prelimsPointers: **15° of longitude = 1 hour**; **1° = 4 minutes** of time.
**Prime Meridian (0°) = Greenwich (GMT)**.
**Indian Standard Time = 82.5°E** (near Mirzapur) = **GMT + 5:30**.
**International Date Line ≈ 180°**; crossing east→west adds a day.
**Summer Solstice (21 Jun)** — Sun over Tropic of Cancer; **Winter Solstice (22 Dec)** — over Tropic of Capricorn.
**Equinoxes (21 Mar, 23 Sep)** — Sun over the Equator; equal day & night worldwide.
Areas near the poles experience **midnight sun / polar night**.
**IST = 82°30'E** (Mirzapur) = **GMT+5:30**; India = single time zone.
**1° longitude = 4 minutes**; **Prime Meridian (Greenwich) = 0° = GMT/UTC**.
**IDL (~180°)**: W→E subtract a day; E→W add a day (zig-zags around land).
Seasons from **axial tilt**; poles get **6-month day/night** (midnight sun).

glossary.definition: Indian Standard Time, based on the 82.5°E meridian, GMT +5:30.
The roughly 180° meridian across which the calendar date changes.
The day the Sun is vertically overhead at a tropic (21 Jun / 22 Dec), giving longest/shortest days.

blocks.text: The Earth's interior is layered into **crust, mantle and core**, revealed mainly by **seismic (earthquake) waves**. Density and temperature rise with depth, and **discontinuities** separate the layers — knowledge central to plate tectonics, volcanism and the magnetic field.

rows: Thin outer shell; **SIAL (continental — Si-Al) over SIMA (oceanic — Si-Mg)**; oceanic crust denser/thinner.
Up to ~2900 km; **asthenosphere** (partly molten, source of magma); convection drives plates.
**Outer core (liquid Fe-Ni)** — generates the **magnetic field**; **inner core (solid)**; the **NIFE** layer.
**P-waves** (primary, through solids & liquids), **S-waves** (secondary, solids only — hence liquid outer core).
Thinnest; basaltic ocean floor, granitic continents.
**Asthenosphere** (upper mantle) — source of magma & plate movement; **Moho** = crust-mantle boundary.
Solid despite heat due to immense pressure; hottest (~5000°C+).

items: **Evidence** = **seismic waves**: **P-waves** (primary, longitudinal, travel through solid+liquid+gas), **S-waves** (secondary, transverse, **not through liquid** → proved the liquid outer core), surface waves (most damage); **shadow zones** map the interior.
**Discontinuities**: **Moho** (crust/mantle), **Gutenberg** (mantle/core), **Lehmann** (outer/inner core).
**Density increases** with depth; the lithosphere = crust + rigid upper mantle (the tectonic plates).
S-waves don't pass the outer core → it's liquid; P-shadow & S-shadow zones prove core structure.
Discontinuities: Moho (crust-mantle), Gutenberg (mantle-core).

prelimsPointers: Three layers — **Crust, Mantle, Core**; studied via **seismic waves**.
**SIAL** (continental crust, Si+Al) over **SIMA** (oceanic crust, Si+Mg); core = **NIFE (Ni+Fe)**.
**Asthenosphere** (upper mantle) — source of magma; convection drives **plate tectonics**.
**Outer core is liquid** → generates Earth's **magnetic field**; **inner core solid**.
**S-waves cannot pass through the liquid outer core** (S-wave shadow zone).
Discontinuities — **Moho (crust-mantle), Gutenberg (mantle-core), Lehmann (inner core)**.
**P-waves** = fastest, longitudinal, travel through all media; **S-waves** = transverse, solids only.
Layers: **Crust → Mantle → Outer core (liquid) → Inner core (solid)**; core = **NiFe**.
**S-waves don't pass through liquids** → proved the **liquid outer core**; P-waves pass all.
Boundaries: **Moho** (crust-mantle), **Gutenberg** (mantle-core), **Lehmann** (inner core).
**Outer core convection** generates Earth's **magnetic field**; asthenosphere feeds volcanism.

glossary.definition: The partly molten upper-mantle layer whose convection drives plate movement.
The boundary between the Earth's crust and mantle.
The region where secondary waves fail to arrive, proving the outer core is liquid.

blocks.text: The Earth's surface displays **first-order (continents, ocean basins), second-order (mountains, plateaus, plains) and third-order (minor erosional/depositional)** landforms, shaped by **endogenic (tectonic/volcanic)** and **exogenic (weathering/erosion)** forces.

rows: **Fold (Himalayas, Alps), Block/fault (Vosges, Sierra Nevada), Volcanic (Fuji), Residual (Aravalli)**.
**River (V-valley, delta), glacier (U-valley, moraine), wind (barchan, loess), sea (cliffs, beaches), groundwater (karst)**.

sections.heading: 🔎 Exam-ready deep coverage: major landforms & processes

items: **Plate tectonics**: lithosphere = **7 major + minor plates**; boundaries — **convergent** (subduction → fold mountains/volcanoes/trenches; **Himalayas** = Indian-Eurasian collision), **divergent** (mid-ocean ridges, sea-floor spreading, rift valleys — **E. African Rift**), **transform** (San Andreas fault). Driven by **mantle convection**; theory built on Wegener's **Continental Drift** & Hess's sea-floor spreading.
**Mountains (3 types)**: **Fold** (Himalayas, Alps, Andes — youngest & highest), **Block/faulting** (Vosges, Black Forest — horst & graben), **Volcanic** (Fujiyama, Kilimanjaro).
**Endogenic (internal)** forces build (tectonism, volcanism); **Exogenic (external)** forces wear down (weathering, erosion by **rivers, glaciers, wind, waves, groundwater**).

**Fluvial (river)**: V-valleys, gorges, waterfalls, meanders, ox-bow lakes, **deltas & floodplains** (deposition). **Glacial**: U-valleys, cirques, moraines, fjords. **Aeolian (wind/desert)**: barchan dunes, mushroom rocks, loess. **Karst (limestone/groundwater)**: caves, stalactites/stalagmites, sinkholes. **Coastal**: cliffs, beaches, spits, lagoons.
**Volcanoes**: active/dormant/extinct; **'Ring of Fire' (Pacific)** = 2/3 of world volcanoes; hotspots (Hawaii).

flowchart TD
  A[Mantle convection] --> B[Plate movement]
  B --> C[Convergent - fold mountains, volcanoes, trenches]
  B --> D[Divergent - mid-ocean ridges, rift valleys]

prelimsPointers: **Fold mountains** — Himalayas, Alps, Andes, Rockies (young); **residual** — Aravalli (old).
**Block mountains** form between **faults (horst & graben — rift valleys)**.

**River landforms** — V-valley, meander, ox-bow lake, **delta** (depositional).
**Glacial** — U-shaped valley, cirque, moraine, fjord; **Aeolian (wind)** — barchan dunes, loess.
**Karst (limestone)** — sinkholes, caves, stalactites/stalagmites.
**Endogenic** forces build (tectonic); **exogenic** forces (weathering/erosion) wear down.
**Convergent** boundary → fold mountains/subduction (**Himalayas**); **divergent** → mid-ocean ridge; **transform** → faults (San Andreas).
Mountains: **Fold** (Himalayas), **Block** (horst-graben), **Volcanic**.
River (fluvial) deposition → **delta/floodplain**; glacial → **U-valley/fjord**; desert → **barchan dunes/loess**; limestone → **karst (stalactites)**.
**Pacific 'Ring of Fire'** = most active volcano-earthquake belt; **Wegener** = Continental Drift.

glossary.definition: A mountain formed by compression and folding of crustal rocks, e.g. the Himalayas.
A graben — a sunken block of land between two faults (e.g. the East African Rift).
Landforms produced by the dissolution of limestone — caves, sinkholes and dripstones.
The plastic upper-mantle layer beneath the lithosphere on which tectonic plates move.
